title: The Bao-Ying Battle in Blossoms Shanghai Was Based on an Illegal Takeover
dek: In 1993, Shenzhen Bao'an used three subsidiaries to buy 4.5% of Yanzhong Industrial each, only filing a disclosure once the combined stake hit 16% — dodging the 5% announcement threshold. The CSRC fined it 1 million yuan but still ruled the acquisition valid: Yanzhong Industrial really was bought out.
why: Liang Jie of Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, as both a Shanghai native and an economist, maps the show's Bao-Ying battle, Mr. A and Uncle Ye one by one onto real history — the institutional details are harder than the plot.
who: People who watched Blossoms Shanghai and want to know what was fact, plus investors and practitioners interested in the early institutional evolution of China's securities market.
skip: From 1:03:29 to 1:08:33, on personal memories of middle school and university and the anxieties of young people — not closely tied to the stock market thread.

points.h: When the exchange reopened there were only eight stocks
points.body: Shanghai shut its stock exchange in 1949 and issued its first stock in 1984, but once you bought shares there was nowhere to trade them. In 1986 a storefront of a dozen-odd square meters on Nanjing Road near Xikang Road — said to have been a barbershop — was converted into an ICBC trading point, with a blackboard listing that day's prices and only two stocks. The Shanghai Stock Exchange formally reopened in 1990 with just eight stocks, and anyone anywhere in the country who wanted to buy had to come to Shanghai. Even whether shares should be paper certificates or electronic was fiercely debated — many people felt uneasy without a piece of paper in hand.

points.h: T+3 was forced into existence by hand-counting stock certificates
points.body: At first the rule was T+3: three days after selling, you got your money, because the certificates handed in had to be counted every day — a thousand or ten thousand of them, one by one, and until the count was clear no payment could be made. Then they found there were too many certificates: forget T+3, even T+13 wasn't enough to finish counting, and no amount of overtime could get through the nightly count, so exchange leaders finally decided to go online and paperless. Computers were just emerging then and many people were skeptical. Price limits didn't exist at first either; the initial limits were stricter than today's, but when they found the restrictions so tight that no one had incentive to come in and buy, they were scrapped for a period after 1993 and price swings became extremely violent, until new limits were set again after 1996.

points.h: Almost all the earliest stock market entrants were washed out
points.body: In the show, Bao Zong was born around Sinan Road and Gaolan Road in the French Concession, the descendant of a capitalist, and entered the market to prove himself after his first love Xuezhi decided he had no future. In reality, the first wave of people who made money in the stock market from the late 1980s to the early 1990s were a mixed lot: not-very-busy traditional Chinese medicine doctors, university teachers who weren't so busy in the early 1990s, well-connected journalists, vocational-school teachers of finance and business. What the TV drama cannot fully show, Liang Jie points out, is that this group was largely washed out by the late 1990s, going bankrupt, vanishing or even committing suicide for various reasons — people who could stand firm in the market for decades almost did not exist.

points.h: Yang Baiwan only kept his money by buying property
points.body: Yang Baiwan was the emblematic figure who first entered the stock market by trading treasury bonds and made a lot of money. In the 1980s a "ten-thousand-yuan household" was already considered well off; he had a million, which in the early 1990s was formidable. But after ups and downs he was not very successful in the market later on; fortunately he put the money he had made into real estate, and when he died in his seventies he may have had ten million or several tens of millions. Liang Jie calls this a relatively happy ending, but notes that Yang recalled many friends and colleagues who struggled alongside him in the market and quickly disappeared from it in the 1990s or early 2000s for various reasons.

points.h: The Bao-Ying battle is based on the Bao-Yan affair
points.body: The heavily dramatized Bao-Ying battle is based on Yanzhong Industrial, one of Shanghai's Old Eight, which Shenzhen Bao'an Group wanted to acquire. The 1993 Interim Regulations on the Administration of Stock Issuance and Trading required disclosure once an acquisition of target shares reached 5% directly or indirectly, with another disclosure for every additional 2% and a mandatory interval between them. But the Bao'an camp had three subsidiaries each buy separately — 4.5%, 4.8% each — already far past 5% combined, and only filed once the total reached 16%. Only then did Yanzhong Industrial discover that its largest shareholder had become Bao'an, and it immediately complained to regulators about a hostile takeover.

points.h: A 1 million yuan fine, and the acquisition still ruled valid
points.body: In October 1993 the CSRC and the Shanghai Stock Exchange launched a joint investigation into the Bao-Yan acquisition. The result was a warning and a 1 million yuan fine for Bao'an, warnings for the related parties, but most crucially the Bao'an camp's acquisition of Yanzhong shares was ruled valid. In the show both sides back off and everyone is happy; in history Yanzhong Industrial really was successfully acquired by Shenzhen Bao'an, which was soon itself hit by a tender offer from Peking University Founder on the secondary market, and the company essentially became Founder Technology. Liang Jie says that even when regulators step in, they cannot say you may not acquire — they can only fine you, criticize and educate — and in the end the acquisition still had to be recognized as valid.

points.h: The production team wanted to recreate the 1993 candlestick charts
points.body: Before Blossoms Shanghai started shooting, a friend on Wong Kar-wai's team invited Liang Jie for tea, and he saw two bookshelves in the office filled entirely with 1990s Shanghai books on stocks, finance and economics, while another team specialized in researching 1990s food, clothing, housing and daily life. They wanted his help recreating 1990s candlestick charts: for example, accurately reproducing a given stock's intraday movement on October 5, 1993. But candlestick charts need high-frequency data, minute-by-minute prices, and the 1990s simply didn't have that much data — finding the opening and closing prices was already good. Substituting a 2005 chart for a 1993 one would be inaccurate, and after a long discussion they couldn't come up with a good solution; in the end they may have changed approach and not drawn candlestick charts directly.

points.h: Blossoms Shanghai may have extended the life of Shanghainese by 50 years
points.body: After Blossoms Shanghai aired, many post-2000 students wanted to talk to Liang Jie about 1990s Shanghai, even though they had grown up in the city and knew nothing about the decade. Liang Jie says Shanghainese has been declining for at least 20 years; more than 50% of Shanghai's population are migrants, and even children of two Shanghainese parents don't speak it well or speak it non-standard — the Shanghainese of the post-90s generation is already very dubious, and the post-2000s generation barely speaks it at all. A friend said something that struck him deeply: it is precisely because Blossoms Shanghai exists that the life of the Shanghainese language can be extended by 50 years.
